I started running again in March. Not for any big reason. My knee had stopped hurting and the mornings were finally light enough that I didn't need a headlamp on the river path.

The first week was bad. Two kilometres, walk, two more, and then a day off that turned into three. What got me back out was a stupid thing: a heron that stands in the same spot by the weir most mornings, and I wanted to see if it was there. It usually is.

I don't track pace any more. I tried, for about a year, and all it did was make me skip runs when I knew they'd be slow. Now I run to the heron and back, which is about six kilometres, and on Sundays I go past it to the bridge. That's the whole plan.

People ask if I'm training for something. I'm not. I think the honest answer is that running is the only forty minutes of the day when nobody can reach me and I'm not looking at a screen, and I'd do it even if it were bad for me.

If there is advice in here it's this: pick a landmark, not a number.
note: generic topic, plain voice, first-hand detail (the heron)

text:
Some notes on getting things done, mostly for myself.

I've read enough productivity books to know they all say the same three things: write it down, do the hard thing first, and don't check email before lunch. I agree with all three and do none of them consistently. What actually works for me is much dumber.

I keep one text file. It's called todo.txt because I couldn't be bothered to think of a name. Every morning I delete what's done and move the oldest undone item to the top, and then I have to either do it or admit I'm not going to. About a third of the time I admit it. That's fine. That's the point of the exercise.

The second thing is that I stopped having a calendar for anything I can't be fired for missing. Dentist, yes. "Review architecture doc," no. If it matters it's in the file, and the file is one screen long, so I see it.

The third thing is that none of this survives a bad week, and I've stopped pretending it should. When I come back after a bad week I delete the file and start over. Nobody has ever noticed.

This is not a system. I'm suspicious of people who have systems.
note: productivity is a slop-heavy topic; this is a person

text:
Remote work, three years in

We went remote in 2023 when the lease ran out and nobody wanted to sign a new one. I was against it. I'd like that on the record because the rest of this post is going to sound like a convert.

The thing nobody told me is that the loss isn't the meetings. The loss is the thirty seconds after the meeting, where someone says "that was weird, right?" and you find out what everyone actually thinks. We tried to recreate it with a Slack channel. It doesn't work; nothing said in writing is the same as something said while putting on a coat.

What we gained is more concrete. Two of the best people on the team live in cities we would never have opened an office in. Our support engineer works a split shift around school pickup and is the happiest I've seen anyone at this company. And I get an hour and a half a day back, which I mostly spend cooking badly.

I still think we lost something. I think we'd lose more by going back. Both of those are true, and if your company is pretending only one of them is, they're lying to you.
note: opinion the author could be wrong about, first-hand

text:
Why I left consulting after six years

Short version: the work was fine, the people were good, and I was bored in a way that was starting to look like depression.

Longer version. Consulting teaches you to become competent at something in three weeks and then leave. I got very good at the three weeks. What I never got was the year after, where the thing you built either works or doesn't and you have to live with it. By year four I noticed I couldn't name a single system I'd shipped that I knew was still running.

I'm now an engineer at a logistics company with about ninety people. My salary went down by roughly a fifth. My sleep went up by roughly an hour. I own a scheduling service that breaks in interesting ways every few weeks, and I know exactly why each time, which is a kind of satisfaction I'd forgotten existed.

I don't recommend this for everyone. If you like the three weeks, consulting is the best job in the world. I just found out, late, that I don't.

text:
Retrieval latency, not model size, predicts user abandonment in conversational search

Abstract. We study 2.1 million sessions from a deployed conversational search assistant over eight weeks (June to July 2026) to ask which system properties predict a user abandoning a session before receiving an answer. Controlling for query type and time of day, a 500 ms increase in retrieval latency raises abandonment by 3.4 percentage points (95% CI 3.1 to 3.7), while swapping the 8B generator for the 70B generator changes abandonment by 0.2 points (CI -0.1 to 0.5), a difference within noise. The latency effect is nonlinear: below 800 ms total time-to-first-token it is flat, and above 1.6 s it steepens. We replicate the main result on a second product with 340,000 sessions. We release the anonymised session logs and analysis code. Our findings suggest that for interactive retrieval systems, engineering effort on the retrieval path yields larger user-facing gains than generator scaling at current model sizes.

Council awards ferry contract to Norse Maritime after two failed tenders

The Harbour City Council voted 7 to 4 on Tuesday to award the ten-year cross-harbour ferry contract to Norse Maritime, ending eighteen months in which two earlier tenders collapsed.

The contract, worth $184 million according to the tender documents published on the council's procurement portal, requires Norse to replace the current diesel fleet with four battery-electric vessels by 2029. Norse's bid was the only one of three finalists to commit to the 2029 date; the others proposed 2031 and 2032.

Councillor Priya Nair, who voted against, told the Post the decision "locks us into one operator before the charging infrastructure exists". Council's own infrastructure report, tabled in June, estimates the shore-side charging at a further $31 million, which is not included in the contract.

Norse Maritime's chief executive Lars Henriksen said in a statement that the company "has operated electric ferries in Bergen since 2021 and will bring that experience here". The previous operator, Harbour Ferries, did not bid. Its parent company entered administration in February.

The first electric vessel is due for sea trials in late 2028.

text:
The last typesetter in Kanda

Yoshio Maeda is 81 and still sets type by hand, six days a week, in a shop his father opened in 1952. There are, by his count, three people in Tokyo who can still do what he does. Two of them are his apprentices, and both are over sixty.

The shop is the width of a car. Cases of type run floor to ceiling on both walls, around fifty thousand pieces, most of them cast before 1970. When a character wears out he casts a new one from a matrix in the back, on a machine he bought in 1968 and has repaired himself ever since. "There is no one to call," he says.

His customers are wedding invitations, a handful of small presses, and, lately, design students who want to touch the process. He charges them the same as anyone. Orders are up, he says, for the first time in twenty years, though "up" means eleven a month instead of eight.

I asked what happens to the type when he stops. He pointed at the shelves. "Someone will want it. Or the metal is worth something." Then he went back to the case he was working on, and did not look up again for a while.

Study finds microplastic levels in Tokyo Bay flatfish unchanged since 2019

A five-year monitoring study by the Tokyo Metropolitan Fisheries Research Institute has found no significant change in microplastic particle counts in flatfish caught in Tokyo Bay between 2019 and 2024, despite the introduction of Japan's plastic resource circulation law in 2022.

The study, published on Monday in Marine Pollution Bulletin (doi:10.1016/example), sampled 1,240 fish across 14 sites. Mean counts were 4.1 particles per fish in 2019 and 3.9 in 2024, a difference the authors describe as within sampling error.

Lead author Dr. Aiko Nishimura said the result was "not surprising", since most particles found were polyethylene fragments consistent with degradation of plastic already in the bay rather than new inputs. "Reducing new plastic is necessary but the bay will take decades to respond," she said.

Prof. Martin Keller of the University of Hamburg, who was not involved, cautioned that the site selection excludes the Arakawa river mouth, where earlier surveys found the highest concentrations. "A flat trend elsewhere doesn't rule out a rise there," he said.

Rust vs Go in 2026: A Balanced Perspective

In today's rapidly evolving software landscape, choosing the right programming language is more important than ever. Rust and Go have both emerged as popular choices for modern backend development, each with its own strengths and trade-offs. In this article, we'll take a balanced look at both.

Performance
Rust is known for its zero-cost abstractions and memory safety without garbage collection, making it a strong choice for performance-critical applications. Go, on the other hand, offers a garbage collector and a simpler concurrency model with goroutines, which can be more than sufficient for many use cases.

Developer Experience
Go's simplicity is one of its greatest strengths. Its minimal syntax and fast compile times make it easy to learn and productive to use. Rust has a steeper learning curve due to its ownership model, but many developers find that the compiler's guidance ultimately leads to more robust code.

Ecosystem
Both languages have vibrant ecosystems. Rust's Cargo and crates.io provide excellent tooling, while Go's standard library is famously comprehensive.

Conclusion
Ultimately, the choice between Rust and Go depends on your specific needs. Both are excellent languages, and the best choice is the one that aligns with your team's goals and expertise. Whichever you choose, you'll be well positioned for success in 2026.

text:
5 Leadership Lessons from Ernest Shackleton

Ernest Shackleton's Endurance expedition of 1914 to 1917 remains one of the most remarkable stories of leadership in history. When his ship was trapped and crushed by Antarctic ice, Shackleton led all 27 of his men to safety over nearly two years. Here are five leadership lessons we can learn from his journey.

1. Put People First
Shackleton prioritised the wellbeing of his crew above all else. In today's workplace, leaders who genuinely care about their teams build trust and loyalty.

2. Stay Optimistic
Despite overwhelming odds, Shackleton maintained a positive outlook. Optimism is contagious and helps teams persevere through challenges.

3. Be Adaptable
When the original goal became impossible, Shackleton redefined success as bringing everyone home. Great leaders know when to pivot.

4. Lead by Example
Shackleton shared the hardships of his men, taking on the same tasks and rations. Leaders earn respect by doing, not just directing.

5. Communicate Clearly
Shackleton kept his crew informed and involved in decisions. Clear communication reduces uncertainty and builds cohesion.

Conclusion
Shackleton's story continues to inspire leaders today. By applying these timeless lessons, you can navigate your own challenges with resilience and purpose.

Doctors Are Begging People to Stop Using This Common Kitchen Item

There's an item in almost every kitchen that doctors say could be putting your health at risk, and most people have no idea. Read on to find out what it is and why experts are so concerned.

Many of us use this item every single day without thinking twice. It's convenient, it's cheap, and it's been a kitchen staple for decades. But according to some health professionals, it may not be as harmless as we think.

The item in question is the plastic cutting board. Over time, knives create grooves in the plastic where bacteria can build up. Some studies have also raised questions about tiny plastic particles that may be released during cutting.

However, experts also note that with proper cleaning and regular replacement, plastic cutting boards are generally safe for most people. Wooden boards have their own considerations, and the choice often comes down to personal preference.

The bottom line? Keep your cutting boards clean, replace them when they get heavily scarred, and you'll likely be fine.

text:
Retries

tinyq retries a failed job up to `max_retries` times (default 3) with exponential backoff starting at `retry_delay` seconds (default 1). A job fails when its handler raises; a handler that returns normally is acked, whatever it returns.

Backoff is `retry_delay * 2 ** attempt` with full jitter, so the third retry of a job with the defaults waits somewhere between 0 and 8 seconds. Set `retry_jitter=False` to make it deterministic, for example in tests.

Which exceptions retry
By default every exception retries. Pass `retry_on=(TimeoutError, ConnectionError)` to retry only those, or raise `tinyq.Discard` from the handler to drop the job without retrying and without an error log.

After the last retry the job moves to the dead-letter queue named `<queue>.dead`. Nothing consumes it unless you do; `tinyq dead --requeue <queue>` moves everything back.

Note: with the Redis backend, a worker killed with SIGKILL mid-job does not count as a failure. The job's visibility timeout (`visibility=30`) expires and another worker picks it up. That is a redelivery, not a retry, and does not increment the attempt counter. See Delivery semantics.

Weekly Engineering, issue 142

Three things worth your time this week.

1. Postgres 18 is out (postgresql.org/about/news/2026-09-18). The headline feature is asynchronous I/O for sequential scans; the release notes claim up to 3x on cold-cache scans on NVMe. Lukas Fittl's benchmark post (pganalyze.example/blog/pg18-aio) measures 1.4 to 2.1x on a c6i.4xlarge, which is still very good. The `io_method` setting defaults to `worker`; `io_uring` needs a rebuild flag.

2. Cloudflare's incident write-up for the 12 September outage (blog.cloudflare.example/2026-09-12-incident) is the usual honest read: a config push that passed staging because staging had a fifth of the routes. 54 minutes, 8% of requests. The action item that matters is "staging carries a full route table by December".

3. A paper I keep thinking about: "Retrieval latency, not model size, predicts user abandonment in conversational search" (arxiv.example/abs/2609.04412). Two million sessions; 500 ms of retrieval latency costs more users than swapping an 8B model for a 70B one. If you own a RAG product, argue about this with your team.

That's it. Reply and tell me what I missed.
